explanation: No single theme. The most consistent cue is the Hacker News comment separator '======\n' that follows a URL line, but it also fires strongly on unrelated tokens: code loop bounds ('names.length', ' <', '0,'), word-piece tokens inside names and biomedical terms ('apolipoprotein E', 'metaiodo', '4q25', 'Ebbsfleet'), and stray tokens like 'jquery[ui]' and 'As you can see'. Weak activations land on ordinary function words.

Fires on the first subword piece that starts a proper name, product name or rare word once that word has been split into pieces (e.g. 'Nich'olson, '-H'odgkin, 'Suh'ayla, 'P'altrow, 'L'inq, 'N'MC, 'Bis'accia), in any language. It is strongest on the word-initial fragment rather than on whole common words. Ordinary function words give at most weak activation.

Fires on tokens inside citation and reference apparatus: 'al' in 'et al.', pieces of bracketed reference keys like '[@B10', '[@CR15', citation-number digits, the year inside a citation, legal-reporter parentheticals like '(orig. proceeding)', and the '(' of disambiguation entries such as 'David (surname)' or 'Liu Shan (207–'. Ordinary prose stays weak.

Fires mostly on punctuation and syntax tokens inside code, shell commands, LaTeX and URLs (the '}{' in '\stackrel{d}{=}', '&', '(*', '}', ' \;', '/group', '/android'). There is a separate weaker cluster on ' of' in 'the southern tip of <place>'. Activations are moderate overall, and only one example passes 60%.

A diffuse mix. The strongest hit is ' =' in an Elixir pattern match. Other hits are word-initial pieces of tech or product names ('key'tool, ' rsa', 'D'ataloader, 'Big'Commerce), prepositions after lab methods ('immunoblot using', 'Western blots with'), and assorted function words. No shared context predicts it well.

Fires on a word just after a negating, limiting or quantifying word, or inside a set phrase, where that word is close to predictable: 'Nothing could', 'WITHOUT WARRANTIES', 'so we can', 'do not respond', 'poor egg quality', 'few things', 'nothing could be'. It also fires on nouns in phrases like 'gross income' and 'revenue growth'. The context matters more than the token's identity.

Fires mainly on the first subword piece of a word split into pieces, especially in legal or formal text: 'rem'and, 'rem'edy, 'Att'orneys, 'am'eliorate, '-ap'pearance, 'carr'erai, 'Lux'emburgo. It also fires on assorted tokens in Italian, French and legal boilerplate ('and is hereby certified'). Whole common words give weak activation.

Fires on a middle digit token inside a multi-digit number: the second digit of a percentage or count ('5[3].3%', '4[4].5%', '13,[4]00', '5,[3]76', port numbers like '7[4]12'). Activation needs a preceding digit in the same number. Mid and weak hits are unrelated words.

Fires on subword fragments in the middle of rare names or foreign words ('Be[itr]ag', 'G[elf]ond', 'dox[yc]ycline', 'as[cor]bate', 'Bol[iv]ian', 'Dj[oh]ar') and on the token right after 'NO.' in court docket numbers or before model and version numbers ('Dell 922', 'BMP280'). The shared thread is tokens in the middle of an unfamiliar or alphanumeric string.

A mixture. It fires on the second or later piece of an all-caps dateline city name ('SANTA CL[ARA]', 'ANCH[ORAGE]', 'J[ACK]SON HEIGHTS', 'PETERSBUR[G]'), on digits in timestamps and dates ('+0[0]00', 'August [2]'), on a Go struct-closing newline, and on scattered other words ('higher then', 'doesn't matter').

Fires on the verb or particle that completes an act of joining or arriving at a group or place: 'joined', 'join', 'rejoin', 'came to', 'come over to', 'stopped by', 'show up'. The top hits are 'joined <team/group>' and 'came to <country/city>'. Weaker hits are 'back' or 'to' after other motion verbs.

Fires on ' to' that starts a purpose or goal clause, or marks the target of a transfer, right after a noun phrase or object ('I'm using the code below to retrieve', 'refer your code to', 'converting jQuery code to HTML5', 'complete this form to'). Moderate hits are other prepositions ('in', 'on') in similar spots.

Fires on syntax tokens inside styling or attribute assignments in CSS, SVG, XAML or plotting code, especially the '="', ':', 'px', or quote token right before a color, border or style value (stroke-width=", border: 1px, textDecoration: "underline", color: 'yellow'). Activation is strongest when the context involves colors or visual styling.

Fires mainly on '.S' in the U.S.C. statute citation ('42 U.S.C.'). It also fires on assorted tokens inside URLs, file paths and code boilerplate ('/', 'httpdocs', '/core', '@since', 'frame'), and on a few prose nouns ('peace officer', 'component').
